description: Cross-skill transfer edges for BKT initialisation. When a source skill is mastered, target skills receive a p_learned boost of (source_p_learned × weight). These are PROPOSED edges — review and adjust weights before enabling in production.

edges.rationale: Counting to 20 provides the conceptual foundation for equal groups (multiplication). Students who can count fluently model groups by counting.
Make-10 strategy requires complementary thinking (what do I add to reach 10?), which directly enables finding the difference by counting up.
Addition with regrouping and subtraction with borrowing share the same place-value exchange concept. Mastering one strongly predicts readiness for the other.
Two-digit subtraction with borrowing is the direct prerequisite for three-digit operations; regrouping across both operations uses identical reasoning.
Three-digit addition/subtraction fluency supports multi-digit multiplication — students who can handle 3-digit operations have the place-value confidence for column multiplication.
Rectangular arrays directly model division. A student who understands a 3×4 array naturally sees that 12 ÷ 3 = 4. This is the strongest transfer edge in early multiplication/division.
Knowing the ×2, ×5, ×10 tables enables immediate recall of corresponding division facts (inverse relationship).
Mastering all multiplication tables up to 12×12 directly enables short division with known facts.
Multi-digit multiplication (long multiplication) shares the column-by-column structure of long division.
Understanding unit fractions (1/n) provides the conceptual bridge to decimal tenths and hundredths (1/10, 1/100). Fraction intuition transfers strongly to decimal notation.
Fraction addition requires finding equivalent fractions, which is the same core skill needed for ratio equivalence and proportion.
Fraction equivalence (2/4 = 1/2) is the same multiplicative reasoning used in ratio and proportion (2:4 = 1:2).
Decimal multiplication and division (×10, ÷100) supports direct proportion calculations involving scale factors.
Operations on negative numbers are a prerequisite concept for understanding integer solutions and the full number line used in algebra.
Mastering negative numbers and integers (including BODMAS) is the gateway to algebraic thinking — variables extend the number system students already know.
Simplifying algebraic expressions is the core manipulation skill underlying all linear equation solving.
Expanding brackets is directly used when rearranging linear equations with brackets.
Solving linear equations (ax + b = c) is the direct precursor to quadratic methods; students who understand inverse operations can extend to factoring.
Plotting and interpreting straight-line graphs develops coordinate fluency used in trigonometric graphs.
Quadratic factoring and the quadratic formula appear frequently in advanced problem-solving contexts.
Trigonometric identities and functions appear in many advanced problem-solving questions.
Syllable segmentation (breaking words into chunks) is an auditory precursor to letter-sound mapping. Students who can segment syllables are cognitively ready to map individual phonemes to letters.

Full phoneme segmentation (saying each sound individually) is the strongest phonological predictor of letter-sound mastery. If a student can segment /k/-/æ/-/t/, they are ready to map each phoneme to its letter.
Bidirectional phoneme awareness (segment AND blend) directly enables bidirectional letter-sound mapping.
Phoneme manipulation (deletion and substitution) requires holding phoneme sequences in working memory — exactly the skill needed to decode digraphs as single phoneme units.
Letter-to-sound retrieval is the direct prerequisite for digraph decoding — a student who knows individual letter sounds is cognitively ready to learn that two letters can make one sound.
Mastering visually confusable letters (b/d, p/q) indicates visual discrimination precision needed for digraph discrimination.
Digraph retrieval (two letters, one sound) and blend production (two letters, two sounds) are complementary decoding skills — knowing one reduces learning time for the other.
Consonant blend production builds the phonological awareness needed to recognise how suffixes attach to base words without disrupting the blend.
Common suffix awareness (–ed, –ing, –ly) is the direct precursor to decoding complex consonant clusters that often contain these suffixes.
Decoding complex clusters is the final alphabetic code skill before CVC/CVCC word reading becomes fluent. Mastery here significantly reduces cognitive load for connected text reading.
CVC word decoding fluency reduces the cognitive load on working memory, freeing capacity for sight word recognition patterns.
Sight word automaticity frees working memory for comprehension processes like sequencing events and identifying main ideas.
Sequencing and identifying the main idea are prerequisite comprehension skills for making inferences — a student who cannot sequence events will struggle to infer cause and effect.
Making inferences about character motivations is the direct cognitive precursor to identifying author intent — both require reading 'beyond the text'.
Understanding cause-and-effect relationships in texts is the analytical foundation needed for critical reading of argument and evidence.
Text structure awareness (compare/contrast, problem/solution) transfers directly to evaluating the structure of persuasive vocabulary.
Identifying author intent is the prerequisite for critical reading — evaluating whether an argument is reliable requires first understanding what the author is trying to do.
Critical reading (evaluating evidence) and synthesising across multiple texts share the same analytical mindset; mastery of one significantly accelerates the other.
